highlights.summary: Kakul Srivastava is the CEO of Splice, the sample platform countless producers rely on for one-shots and melodic loops. Samples pulled from the service have found their way into massive hits like Lisa's " Money " and " Espresso " by Sabrina Carpenter.
body: As head of Splice, Kakul has tried to carefully thread the line on AI music tools. She also hates her cup warmer.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Before that, Kakul held executive roles at Flickr, Yahoo, GitHub, and Adobe. Throughout her career, Kakul has found herself at the intersection of Silicon Valley and creatives. That’s been especially true at Splice, where she’s not just expanded the platform’s footprint by acquiring Spitfire Audio, but also overseen its forays into the world of generative AI.

Last year, she was very outspoken on an episode of Decoder about avoiding the sort of “push-button, get-song” AI that has made companies like Suno so controversial. And based on her answers to our questionnaire, it doesn’t seem like her skepticism has waned. When it comes to Splice, the company has made a point of trying to offer AI products that still keep the human at the center of the creative process. And when it comes to communicating with colleagues, Kakul sees the same need to keep AI at bay.

highlights.title: 'Lanterns' Makes Even More Sense If You Know About DC's Iconic 20-Year-Old Meme
highlights.summary: HBO Max's Lanterns has made the cosmic side of the DC Universe more popular than it's been in a while. Largely due to the adventures of the Green Lantern Corps, DC has a well-established galactic scene, full of feuding aliens, killer robots, space cops, and a giant wall made from dead gods that…
body: Some of that's a little too out there for a live-action TV show, but Lanterns still packs a great deal into its first season, including a reference to the planet-sized Green Lantern Mogo. Notably, it did remember to include the most important part of the entire Green Lantern mythos: Hal Jordan spends a lot of time unconscious.

Through sheer coincidence, the first episode of Lanterns came out a month after the 20-year anniversary of one of the internet comic book community's longest running gags: the Hal Jordan Head Injury Project. More surprisingly, due to the inexplicable immortality of both Flickr and Blogspot accounts, most of the HJHIP is still online today.

Put together by "Sleestak," who still blogs occasionally at Lady, That's My Skull, the HJHIP is a tongue-in-cheek tracker of the sheer number of times that Hal Jordan, in his nearly 70-year history as a character, has taken a shot to the dome.

The best/worst part of the HJHIP is that two of the greatest Hal Jordan skull cracks aren't currently in the archive. The best one that is, however, might be from a particularly wild Silver Age story.

body: The Filter US is turning one. Over the past year, we have cooked, cleaned, hiked and generally put our homes and bodies through a lot in pursuit of things actually worth buying. We have tested packing cubes on 14 trips, spent 63 nights testing sleep masks, recruited 84 coffee drinkers to taste instant coffee and put thousands of products through their paces (and called out ones which we don’t recommend ).

And we have gone deeper: asking a food lab to test the best non-toxic pans, blind-tasting everything from protein bars to nonalcoholic beer and getting the tea on Padma Lakshmi’s favorite kitchen tools. Across hundreds of articles, we have covered everything from a satisfyingly bouncy $1,600 organic mattress to a small but mighty $9 cleaning brush. We have found the legitimately best deals on our favorite things too.

One year in, we wanted to know which things should earn a permanent place in your homes. So we pulled the 25 items our readers have loved most since the Filter US launched – then went back to the writers who originally tested them. Did the products survive months of real life? Would our testers still recommend them to you?

highlights.title: Computational tools for society’s most complex challenges
highlights.summary: Associate Professor Cathy Wu uses reinforcement learning to help map out improvements to transportation and other multifaceted systems.
body: As far back as she can remember, Cathy Wu ’12, MNG ’13 wanted to find ways to solve problems to improve people’s lives. Her parents were Taiwanese immigrants, and her father had a long commute to his job, which took him away from the family. On a tight budget, the rest of the family often stayed home on a street that was too busy for playing outdoors. Wu and her siblings ended up playing a lot of computer games.

Wu says her desire to make the world a better place, her dad’s daily battle against traffic, and the games she played, like “SimCity,” were the seeds of her motivation to design safe, efficient transportation systems.

Wu is an associate professor in the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering (CEE) and the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS), and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. Her research focuses on using machine learning and reinforcement learning (RL) to advance reliable strategies for improving a range of complex systems, including transportation.

highlights.title: Capcom plans to evolve RE Engine into an "AI-generation game engine"
highlights.summary: Capcom wants to transform its in-house RE Engine into what it's calling an "AI-generation game engine".
body: As reported by gamebiz (via VGC ), programmer Satoshi Ishida outlined the plans at the "Capcom Open Conference RE:2026" event yesterday (2nd October), explaining that the changes were coming as part of an ongoing overhaul dubbed the REX Project.
RE Engine has been in development since 2014 and made its debut in Resident Evil 7 back in 2017. It's since been the engine behind the best part of 30 Capcom titles.

Ishida pointed to three challenges driving the REX Project – one, games have grown so large in scope and data volume that build and iteration times are slowing development down; two, RE Engine is now used by over 2,000 developers, including international staff and people coming from other engines, requiring better multilingual and accessibility support; and three, AI needs to be built into the development pipeline rather than bolted on.

That's why Capcom intends to bundle several new systems into the REX Project, including RE:Dox, which standardises data processing across formats, RE:UI, which speeds up development tools by separating appearance from state, and RE:Log, which swaps text-based logging for an ID-based system.
points: Capcom wants to transform its in-house RE Engine into what it's calling an "AI-generation game engine".

highlights.title: Video Games Europe hits back at EU watchdog targeting King, Supercell, Mojang and more over IAP practices
highlights.summary: The EU’s Consumer Protection Cooperation Network has launched coordinated enforcement actions against games companies including King, Supercell, Mojang, Riot Games, Activision Blizzard and Ubisoft, over how they sell and handle in-game virtual currencies.
body: The CPC Network brings together national consumer protection authorities from across the EU and EEA and is coordinated by the European Commission. In a joint statement published September 30, it said it had found that “a high number of video game companies” had made no substantive changes to their practices since it published non-binding “Key Principles” on in-game currencies in March 2025, despite extensive subsequent talks with industry bodies.

It said the coordinated actions are particularly focused on compliance around variable reward systems such as loot boxes, “dark patterns” and other “harmful influencing techniques”, and practices that directly exhort children to spend money, which it says EU law already prohibits.
Video Games Europe and the European Game Developers Federation pushed back on the CPC Network’s actions in a statement also published on September 30.

highlights.title: My relationship with food was broken. Then I killed my own dinner
highlights.summary: For years, eating was something to control, fear or regret. After I hunted my first deer, I started to see fat, hunger and my own body in a different light. I muffled my sobs with a pillow so my family couldn’t hear me from the adjacent room.
body: Pulling tear-soaked strands of hair off my cheeks, I stood in front of a full-length mirror and grabbed the fat of my thighs. If only I could just – I pictured ripping off fistfuls of my body and flinging them out the windows, where they would land on some unknowing French person six stories below. I had this vision often: pulling bits of myself off and casting them somewhere far away from me.

For years, spanning my teens and 20s, eating was either an indulgence to regret or a strategy to overplan. In high school, I chugged 32 ounces of cold green tea every morning, hoping it would burn belly fat like Instagram told me it would. While working at a deli one summer, I ate two bagel sandwiches each shift until my friend mentioned I was eating the carbohydrate equivalent of 10 slices of bread. My daily bagel intake promptly plummeted to zero. I forced myself to choke down a can of tuna in my college dorm before predawn weightlifting sessions. In my early 20s, I started experimenting with intermittent fasting: no food from 8pm until noon the next day.
points: For years, eating was something to control, fear or regret.
After I hunted my first deer, I started to see fat, hunger and my own body in a different light.

highlights.title: An OpenAI safety employee has quit and is sounding the alarm
highlights.summary: David Robinson used to write the safety reports that accompanied every major model release at OpenAI. This week, he resigned from his position and is now speaking out in an editorial in The Atlantic.
body: It’s understandable if you’re feeling a bit cynical about everyone suddenly coming out of the woodwork to warn about how dangerous the thing they helped build is. They did, after all, make this mess. But that doesn’t mean we should discount their warnings.

Robinson says that the culture in industry is fundamentally broken. That this is a deeper issue than simply slapping a few new rules or regulations on how we handle training models. Silicon Valley has operated with “extreme confidence” and “perpetual sprints,” he says, building bigger and better models with “unimpeded optimism” that ignores or underestimates potential problems.

Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.

highlights.title: Resident Evil Dev Capcom Plans To Embrace AI In Game Development
highlights.summary: A Capcom developer recently made some eyebrow-raising statements about integrating AI into RE Engine, the game engine Capcom uses to make games like Resident Evil Requiem, Pragmata, and Onimusha: Way of the Sword.
body: These surprising statements came from programmer Satoshi Ishida at Capcom Open Conference RE: 2026, a tech conference that the company holds to showcase developments on the RE Engine. Reported on first by GameBiz and translated by IGN, Ishida discussed the REX Project, which is meant to evolve RE Engine "for the next generation."

Many of these improvements aren't AI-related and simply focus on things like data formatting or memory management. That said, Ishida also made comments like "successfully integrating AI technology into development workflows has become an essential condition for streamlining future development," and "our goal is a future where we create games together with AI."

Those statements are certainly red flags if you don't want AI involved in game development, although the kind of AI Ishida refers to differs from generative AI used to create art or other game assets. As of March 2026, Capcom had told investors that it did not plan to use generative AI to create content for its games. Resident Evil Requiem was one of the games used in Nvidia DLSS 5's controversial reveal.

highlights.summary: As a fan of Henri Cartier-Bresson, the Egyptian photographer was determined to capture his own ‘decisive moment’ Mirna Abass regards his small Egyptian city as “heaven for street, travel and documentary photography”.
body: On the day he took this shot, Abass had joined a walk with the Egyptian Camera Crew photography club. Abass works as an agricultural engineer, but describes film and photography as his true passions. Henri Cartier-Bresson is one of his biggest inspirations, and he is often guided by the pioneering photographer’s concept of the decisive moment.

“As we explored the shipyard, I saw this teenage fisher jumping between several boats,” Abass says. “I set up my iPhone 13 to capture these two contrasting boats, side by side, and waited patiently, hoping he might eventually make the jump in front of me. I was elated when he did, and went to show him our very own decisive moment.

“The human element gave a sense of scale, of how large these ships are, and I loved how I captured him leaping from the white ship to the colourful ship,” he adds. “It is almost as if he is escaping from pale life to fruitful life.”

highlights.title: California’s new laws target workers’ biggest fear of AI taking their jobs
highlights.summary: The state, which is home to many AI companies, is one of the first to roll out workplace regulations targeting the technology. California’s laws aimed at protecting workers from the impacts of artificial intelligence could pave the way for broader workplace safeguards across the US as calls for…
body: On Thursday, California governor Gavin Newsom signed a suite of new laws that ban bosses from relying entirely on AI to decide whether to fire workers, using it to predict employees’ emotional states or collecting neural data, meaning the information from electrical signals of someone’s brain or nerves. They also require companies to notify workers if layoffs were caused by AI and prohibit AI surveillance in workplace bathrooms.

The new laws come as workers increasingly worry whether AI will take their jobs, lead to discrimination and increase workplace surveillance. Unions, worker advocates and even some lawmakers pushed for the new rules, a regulatory shift for a technology that has largely developed unchecked. California, home to many of the leading companies developing AI, represents one of the first states to roll out a sweeping set of workplace regulations targeting the technology.

“It’s a turning point,” said Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions, AFL-CIO, who’s been helping leaders across the country write regulations. “It’s really the first time we’re seeing California workers showing the country that we don’t have to accept [this].”

highlights.title: Documenting the tech worker movement
highlights.summary: Writing as a participant and researcher, PhD student JS Tan SM ’22 has co-authored a new book about the rise of tech worker protests and the employer backlash that followed.
body: Despite the “dot-com crash” in 2000, the tech industry remained an attractive career destination for many who believed technology represented the future. The digital age — defined by global connectivity and computers — had firmly taken hold, and over time, the tech industry emerged as a dominant force in the labor market. High-paying jobs for engineers, designers, and professionals across a wide range of fields became increasingly common.
MIT PhD student JS Tan SM ’22 was among those who, upon graduating from Brown University and Rhode Island School of Design in 2015, joined the tech industry.
“A lot of us had this idea that technology, and in particular the technologies related to the internet, had the potential for bringing about a more progressive version of the world,” Tan says.
Google echoed this ethos to its employees with its once-famous motto, “don’t be evil,” as their informal corporate philosophy and code of conduct guideline. They’ve since dropped the tagline.

highlights.title: After a Decade-Plus of Chasing Trends, I Finally Found My Uniform on Savile Row
highlights.summary: My goal: a single garment to get me through formal occasions during the festive season, rather than multiple evening dresses which take up precious New York City closet real estate.
body: My immersion into the menswear landscape happened fast. Within a couple of weeks of accepting a job overseeing the beat for a luxury title—after more than a decade covering womenswear—I was bound for Pitti Uomo. A biannual industry trade show, Pitti has outgrown the walls of the fortezza that houses it, spilling into the narrow streets of Florence in an influencer-heavy scene of suiting aficionados determined to out-peacock each other—100-plus-degree temps in June be damned. But among the occasionally over-the-top spectacles, an invaluable sartorial shift occurred.

I’d long been drawn to tailoring when wanting to feel particularly pulled together, no doubt a result of the ease of the school uniform I donned during my youth. As a fashion journalist, then so focused on writing about trends, I couldn’t fathom having the time or inclination to embrace suiting. Even so, I was far more likely to pair a blazer with jeans. A full suit? It felt wildly archaic and, if I’m being frank, a bit boring.

highlights.title: 3D movies are finally worth watching
highlights.summary: Why am I suddenly buying up every 3D Blu-ray I can find after 3D became one of the biggest tech flops of all time? The technology's finally ready for 3D movies to shine, more than 15 years since James Cameron's Avatar wowed me on the big screen and went on to become the highest-grossing film…
body: I’ve always loved 3D movies, but viewing them was awkward. Walking into a movie theater with a pair of polarized glasses, I would only get half the resolution and roughly half the brightness, since those glasses had to split one reflected image between my two eyes. Almost every 3D technology cuts something you care about in half, whether it’s resolution (see also: Nintendo 3DS) or the refresh rate and flicker you get with active shutter glasses.
But what if you had a full screen for each eye? That’s what video glasses can provide.

Last year, I began testing a pair of Xreal One Pro glasses, which primarily give you a gigantic flat screen, like a private theater, for whatever you plug in. But that screen doesn’t technically need to stay flat. If you press and hold the right button, Xreal can give you independent left and right views for side-by-side (SBS 3D) content. With proper content, you get a full 1080p view for each eye.

There are SBS 3D toggles in popular video player apps for VR headsets like the Meta Quest and Steam Frame, too — and the Apple Vision Pro and upcoming Meta VR Glasses let you natively stream 3D films.
